revision_notes: A single light Exa search for this variable surfaced RURA's official current tariff schedule and multiple World Bank/ESMAP sources on Rwandan electricity affordability, so the row was moved from the fast path (confirm-Unknown) to the full verification path rather than being reconfirmed as Unknown. RURA's tariff notice (effective 1 October 2025) gives a residential lifeline rate of RWF 89/kWh for 0-20 kWh/month, RWF 310/kWh for 20-50 kWh, and RWF 369/kWh above 50 kWh. World Bank GNI per capita (Atlas method) for Rwanda is USD 1,040 (2024), i.e. ~USD 86.7/month. The World Bank Multi-Tier Framework survey (2018 report, based on ~2016-17 data) found average national household consumption of ~20.8 kWh/month and an average bill of RWF 3,513.8 (USD 4.21) under the pre-reform tariff. Recalculating with the current lifeline tariff and average consumption gives a bill of roughly USD 1.40/month, or ~1.6% of monthly GNI per capita (code 4, 'Affordable'); using the higher consumption/blended national average tariff (~USD 0.175-0.18/kWh per GlobalPetrolPrices, Sept 2025) instead gives ~USD 8.75-11/month, or 9-13% of monthly income (code 1-2, 'Expensive'/'Very Expensive'). Because the result is highly sensitive to which consumption benchmark is used as 'basic service', and no source states the affordability ratio directly for Rwanda, a mid-range code of 3 ('Moderate', 3-5%) is recorded but flagged for human review rather than asserted with confidence; a reviewer with access to Rwanda's EICV household budget survey expenditure shares could resolve this more precisely.
revised_comments: Rwanda's electricity tariffs are regulated by the Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority (RURA), which revised end-user tariffs with effect from 1 October 2025. Residential consumers pay a lifeline rate of RWF 89 per kWh for the first 20 kWh consumed per month, rising to RWF 310 per kWh for 20-50 kWh and RWF 369 per kWh above 50 kWh. Rwanda's GNI per capita (Atlas method) stands at USD 1,040 (World Bank, 2024), equivalent to around USD 86.70 per month. A household consuming close to the national average of around 20 kWh per month (World Bank Multi-Tier Framework survey) spends approximately USD 1.40 monthly on electricity, around 1.6% of monthly income, which sits within the affordable range for basic consumption under the World Bank/ESMAP rule of thumb (5% of household budget as the affordability threshold). Consumption above the lifeline block, or the blended national average retail price of around USD 0.175-0.18 per kWh, pushes the cost of a more typical household bill closer to 9-13% of monthly per capita income, within the expensive to very expensive range. Reforms since 2017-18, including the introduction and subsequent widening of the lifeline tariff band, combined with rising per capita income, have improved affordability for low, basic levels of consumption, though electricity costs above the lifeline threshold remain among the highest in the East African region.
